hosts: Erik Townsend (solo; Patrick Ceresna and Massil Beguenane off for summer holiday break)
interviewBody:
### 1. What Money and Reserve-Currency Status Actually Are
Lacalle frames state-issued money as fundamentally government debt — central banks worldwide treat sovereign debt as their lowest-risk reserve asset, a historically recent arrangement people mistake for a permanent law of finance. A reserve currency requires investors and central banks to believe the issuing economy will remain stable and provide real (inflation-beating) returns over time; loss of confidence concretely means that holding a country's long-term debt is generating real (and sometimes nominal) losses.

### 2. Three Limits Governments Have Now Exceeded
Lacalle argues developed-world governments have breached three constraints that historically underpinned currency credibility: (1) the **economic limit** — debt now grows faster than GDP even as stimulus fails to lift productivity growth; (2) the **fiscal limit** — deficits and debt-service burdens have become unsustainable even with central banks holding rates low and buying sovereign debt; and (3) the **inflationary limit** — clearly breached in 2020–2021, when the belief that money supply and debt could expand without consequence proved false, especially in economies that had been most confident of that view.

### 3. Digital Currency: CBDCs vs. Stablecoins as Opposing State Strategies
Lacalle contrasts two government responses to crypto's challenge to centralized money. The European Central Bank, he argues, is pursuing central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) out of anxiety about losing reserve-currency relevance (noting the euro has already lost its #2 reserve-asset ranking to gold), attempting to impose usage by digital means. The Trump administration, by contrast, has banned CBDCs domestically while embracing dollar-backed stablecoins and crypto more broadly — a bet that making the US the "capital of crypto assets" reinforces dollar usage globally, since every stablecoin transaction has a dollar (or other currency) on the other side. He frames CBDCs as effectively state surveillance disguised as money — full central-bank visibility into citizens' transactions, with the attendant risk of using account access to police speech — versus decentralized currencies as tools that discipline government excess by offering citizens a competitive alternative.

### 4. Stablecoins as the "Bridge" — and a Structural Vulnerability
Erik proposes that because stablecoins are Treasury-backed, mass migration of transaction volume into stablecoins puts the system "one computer-programmer epiphany away" from a viable dollar replacement — if the backing were ever swapped from Treasuries to something else, the existing stablecoin transaction rails would carry over. Lacalle agrees stablecoins are the realistic bridge from a centralized to a decentralized system, and argues this dynamic forces (rather than threatens) US fiscal/monetary prudence: the government's strongest defense of dollar reserve status is now to actually behave like a currency worth holding, not to rely on inertia. He also argues attempts to regulate stablecoins into being dollar-exclusive are largely futile, since decentralization is the source of their value — the more durable path for the US is to lead by example as the most credible reserve asset.

### 5. Why Central Banks Are Buying Gold, Not Crypto
Central banks are diversifying away from dollar- and euro-denominated debt because those assets no longer deliver the stability and real returns expected of a reserve asset — but Lacalle argues this is a move within the centralized system (gold poses no threat to a government's own monetary sovereignty), not a move toward decentralization. He views this as somewhat self-contradictory: many of the same governments (he points to the BRICS bloc specifically) encouraging gold accumulation are simultaneously trying to preserve capital controls, currency controls, and government-directed monetary policy — i.e., nostalgia for a pre-reserve-currency-competition world, not a genuine embrace of a decentralized future. He argues the US dollar's reserve role rests specifically on institutional independence, open capital markets, and the absence of capital/currency controls — features a BRICS alternative currency would struggle to replicate given those economies' more state-controlled institutions.

### 6. The Road Ahead: Coexistence, Led by Citizens Not Central Banks
Lacalle expects central banks and governments to resist decentralization as long as possible, since all monetary revolutions historically have been citizen-led with institutions adapting last. His base case is coexistence between fiat currencies and independent (crypto) currencies, with competition between them disciplining government-currency issuers — citing Hayek's *Choice in Currency* thesis that competition between currencies limits governments' incentive to inflate away their own obligations. He frames current fiat-currency comparisons (which currency is "strongest") as really a choice among "lesser evils," since every major fiat currency is losing purchasing power relative to gold even as they fluctuate against each other.

### 7. US Trade Policy and Foreign Relations
Asked about the Trump administration's disruptive approach to trade and international relations, Lacalle argues recent US trade agreements with the EU and other partners demonstrate that no party can fully decouple from the US as a trading and financial partner, forcing pragmatic cooperation despite friction. Since governments across the Eurozone, Japan, the UK, China, and the US have all breached the same economic/fiscal/inflationary limits in different ways, he expects continued mutual need for cooperation to keep the broader monetary system stable — characterizing Trump as a disruptive negotiator seeking leverage rather than someone seeking to fully dismantle the existing system.

### 8. Background
Lacalle is chief economist and fund manager at Tressis, president/CEO of Alpha Strategy Consulting, and a professor of global economics at IE Business School. He is the English-language author of *Freedom or Equality*, *Escape from the Central Bank Trap*, *Life in the Financial Markets*, and *The Energy World Is Flat*, with a forthcoming title, *The New Global Economic Order*. More at dlacalle.com.

hosts: Erik Townsend (solo; Patrick Ceresna off this week)
interviewBody:
### 1. Guest Background
Anderson holds a PhD in chemical engineering (thesis on using miniature lightning/plasma to heal wounds) and is founder/managing director of Timescale Ventures, an early-stage deep-tech and critical-technologies fund investing across advanced nuclear fission and fusion, data-center power, industrial robotics, logistics, mobility, manufacturing, and compute. She is an early investor in Aloe Atomics.

### 2. Nuclear Fission Renaissance: What's Actually Changed
Anderson points to a wave of new small-reactor demonstrations (including recent milestones at Idaho National Lab), continued regulatory progress, and a maturing supply chain. She distinguishes two tracks: restarting older nuclear plants and uprating existing plants' output (potentially the fastest ways to add grid-connected nuclear gigawatts), versus new-build advanced reactors at the smaller (1–20 MW) end of the spectrum, where component integration is happening faster than in traditional large-plant builds.

### 3. Mass Production as the Central Bottleneck-Breaker
Both Anderson and Townsend agree the single most important unlock is true assembly-line mass manufacturing of reactor components (vessels, pumps, instruments, safety systems) — not merely off-site factory fabrication, but Henry-Ford-style repeatable, robotics-assisted production. Anderson notes a standard ~1,000 MW plant (citing Vogtle's cost/schedule overruns as a cautionary example) takes the best builders in the world roughly 5 years even at the high end, whereas smaller mass-manufactured designs could deploy in under two years — better matching a typical ~9-month data-center construction timeline. She also credits the NRC's Part 53 (referred to in conversation as "Part 57") advanced-reactor licensing pathway as a meaningful regulatory unlock distinct from traditional light-water-reactor rules.

### 4. Three Niche Markets for Advanced Nuclear — Plus the Real Opportunity
Townsend frames advanced nuclear (higher-cost, at least initially) as currently finding three buyers able to pay up: (1) military/defense, which de-risks new technology but is inherently limited by base count and export controls; (2) remote/off-grid microreactors (mining sites, Arctic communities) displacing diesel generator fleets — a real but small market, since ~1,000 one-megawatt units would be needed to match a single large reactor; and (3) AI data centers, which Anderson identifies as the largest opportunity by far. She credits hyperscalers specifically with creating bankable nuclear demand by being willing counterparties for 20-year PPAs at ~$100/MWh — aggregating order books across a dozen-plus plants in a way individual, historically hyper-local US utilities (some operating only two to four nuclear plants) never could, making projects financable and creating an export pathway to other countries.

### 5. The US Is Falling Behind on Reactor Exports
Anderson flags that of roughly 80 reactors currently under construction globally, about 60 are Chinese-designed (China is on pace to double installed nuclear capacity within five years, adding 5–10 GW/year under a 10-year plan), with most of the remainder Russian-design (including India's buildout, structured as Indian-led projects with Russian state-owned technology partners). Her view: outside the US, current buyers' realistic choices are essentially China or Russia, with South Korea not yet participating meaningfully. She estimates a US AP1000-class plant started today is roughly a 10-year (optimistically 7-year) proposition, whereas a first small/microreactor reference facility could come online by 2028–2029, after which order books and cost-reduction iteration could follow much faster — creating a pathway to more cost-effective reactors by the early 2030s.

### 6. Nuclear Fuel Supply Chain
Anderson highlights conversion (chemically converting mined uranium into a form that can be enriched) as a acute bottleneck: only about five conversion facilities exist worldwide, the sole US facility is old, and much of the remaining global capacity sits in Russia — from which US executive orders call for a 2028 exit with no fully built-out alternative yet. On enrichment, she sees laser enrichment (following the historical progression from gaseous diffusion to centrifuges) as a promising next step, though not yet proven at scale — citing General Matter and GLE (both near Paducah, KY) working on laser isotope separation, and Hexium (Texas), which uses a lithium-metal-based laser process that avoids fluorine chemistry entirely, an approach she also sees as potentially transferable to rare-earth-element processing.

### 7. Turbine Efficiency: Supercritical CO2
Both guests are enthusiastic about supercritical-CO2 (sCO2) turbines replacing steam (whose thermal efficiency is only ~30%) as the working fluid for converting reactor heat to electricity. Higher achievable pressures let sCO2 turbines be built much smaller, aiding mass manufacturing, while reaching efficiencies up to ~50%. Anderson also flags "bottoming cycle" retrofits — attaching sCO2 turbine stages to existing power generation assets to extract an incremental 10–20%+ more output from already-installed capacity — as a nearer-term application than new-build pairings.

### 8. Nuclear Fusion: Timeline and Cost Debate
Townsend (self-described fusion skeptic relative to Anderson) presses on why fusion deserves attention given advanced fission's more proven path to beating fossil-fuel costs. Anderson's counter: realistic new large fission plants and fusion plants are converging on similar early-2030s commercial timelines once ramp-up is included, so fusion isn't meaningfully "later." She attributes fusion's recent credibility shift to high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets shrinking tokamak-class devices (citing Commonwealth Fusion Systems) from stadium-scale to house-scale, major laser-technology advances (citing Colorado-based Xcimer Energy, whose lineage traces to Star Wars-program laser R&D), and dramatically faster design simulation — all enabling companies like Thea Energy to mass-manufacture small, AI-tunable "pixel" magnets. On cost, she argues fusion could ultimately undercut fission because it eliminates the uranium mining/conversion/enrichment/decommissioning/waste-storage cost stack entirely; on fuel cost specifically, she disputes Townsend's tritium-price ($30M/kg) objection by describing closed-fuel-cycle designs where a lithium "blanket" regenerates tritium from deuterium (abundant in seawater, already used in Canadian CANDU reactors) during operation.

### 9. Fusion Investment Landscape: Integrators vs. Enabling Technology
Anderson sees investable opportunity at both levels — integrated fusion power-plant developers (Commonwealth Fusion Systems, Thea Energy on magnets, Xcimer/"Energy Focused Energy" on lasers) and enabling-technology suppliers, including superconducting-magnet materials makers and spinout applications such as Spinner Energy, which is applying fusion-derived superconducting magnet technology to compact high-density power delivery for data centers and grid infrastructure.

### 10. Silicon Carbide and Wide-Bandgap Semiconductors
Anderson highlights silicon carbide — now cheaper due to EV-industry-driven scale (a nod to Tesla/Musk) — for its high-voltage switching and thermal tolerance, useful both as a power-electronics material and as a chemically resistant reactor cladding/insulator. She points to Halo Industries (silicon-carbide wafering/slicing, applicable to both EVs and chip processing) and to solid-state transformers — a key bottleneck in connecting new power sources (including nuclear) to data centers — as an area where silicon carbide is enabling mass-manufactured, lower-cost, faster-lead-time devices (months/weeks versus years).

### 11. Broader Energy/Materials Themes
Anderson flags additional early-stage investment areas: rare-earth element refining, mining, and magnet production; aluminum refining (most US capacity has left the country, creating a reshoring/recycling opportunity); and technologies to shrink the long lead times for bringing new mines online (relevant to copper, aluminum, and other grid- and electronics-critical materials).

### 12. Data Center Power Delivery at Scale
Anderson describes the practical scale challenge as Nvidia's roadmap pushes toward 800-volt in-rack distribution: a single data-center cabinet may soon draw roughly enough power for ~1,000 homes, while data centers themselves (a 40 MW facility compared to "six Costco/club stores" in footprint) are growing rapidly. Grid interconnection requires presenting a smooth, gradual load profile to utilities even though AI training workloads can swing from 80% to 20% utilization within a second — driving investment in rack-level and pre-grid power-management/smoothing technology, standardized interconnection approaches (to avoid bespoke engineering per data center), demand-aggregation/virtual-power-plant technologies that shave peak load, and geothermal.

### 13. Geothermal: Promising but Not Yet a Mass-Manufacturing Story
Townsend is skeptical that geothermal (which requires drilling to ~400°C rock several thousand meters down, currently only economical at rare surface-accessible sites) can achieve nuclear-style mass-production cost curves, given it resembles a bespoke, fracking-like services model rather than a factory-built product. Anderson agrees this is a real distinction, flags Quaise Energy (deep-drilling technology aimed at reaching high-temperature rock closer to load centers rather than only remote sites) and cites better subsurface modeling/simulation as easing (not solving) the challenge, alongside materials advances (e.g., harder, thermally conductive drill-bit materials shared with mining and data-center applications) as incremental unlocks. She frames herself as agnostic/diversified ("all of the above") across nuclear fission, fusion, and geothermal rather than picking one winner.

### 14. Robotics: Industrial Applications Ahead of Humanoids
Asked to weigh in outside her core expertise, Anderson argues near-term robotics value is concentrated in non-humanoid form factors operating in dangerous, remote, or otherwise human-unfriendly environments — citing Pyka (autonomous crop-dusting/agricultural aircraft, now covering tens of thousands of acres across South and Central America) and Fort Robotics (human-robot workspace safety, in the process of a SPAC transaction) as portfolio examples, alongside broader activity in shipbuilding, decommissioning, and construction robotics. She estimates in-home humanoid robots are still five-plus years out.

### 15. Timescale Ventures
Anderson describes Timescale Ventures' thesis as founded on a maturing "talent stack" (engineers now coming from SpaceX, Rivian, Tesla, and industry with real hardware-company experience) combined with dramatically better tooling — simulation, prototyping, materials, off-the-shelf robotics components — that she credits with making hardware/deep-tech investing viable on venture-fund timescales (the source of the firm's name). The fund invests across advanced nuclear/fusion, data-center power, industrial robotics, logistics, mobility, manufacturing, and compute. More information: timescale.vc and the firm's Substack (handle "timescalevc").

**Bottom line:** Agentic AI is now reliable enough to automate whole "queue-processing" teams. But token bills scale fast, open Chinese models are ~100–500x cheaper, and the debt-financed data-center build-out depends on two customers (OpenAI and Anthropic). Barrie's view: open models plus owned hardware win the token market, and NVIDIA is already pivoting to sell boxes direct.

### 1. Agents Are Replacing Queue Work Now
Barrie runs ~44 self-built agents at Freelancer. They have automated a 24/7, 11-person project-review queue in two short sessions, replaced a $150–200K performance-marketing role with a 4 a.m. daily ads report, and now handle 100% of tier-one customer support. His playbook: go team by team, find the "queue processors," and automate them. The future team is a team leader plus AI.

### 2. Token Costs Are the Real Constraint
One day burned 4 billion tokens (~$1,300, mostly Claude Sonnet). That would have been ~$80K on an Opus-class model without prompt caching. The same workload on Chinese open models (GLM 5.3, DeepSeek) would cost ~$150, a ~500x spread across models with zero switching costs. The catch is that hosted cheap models train on your data.

### 3. Own the Hardware: "Not My AI, Not My Data"
Barrie bought eight NVIDIA DGX Sparks (~$4–5K each, ~100W). A pair runs DeepSeek V4 Flash at near-Opus quality. A 16-box cluster (~$65K) would cover his whole agent workload for ~$100/day amortized. Sparks, Mikrotik switches and RTX 6000s are sold out globally, and GPU/server resale is becoming Escrow.com's #2 category. He expects an enterprise "emperor has no clothes" moment over cloud AI privacy.

### 4. The Data-Center Debt Bomb
Citing Ed Zitron: hyperscalers have taken on ~$1.65T of debt in five years (vs. $1.3T subprime peak), much of it in off-balance-sheet SPVs (e.g., Meta's ~$46B Hyperion exposure). OpenAI and Anthropic are ~73–74% of Amazon's and Microsoft's AI revenue. "Teaser-rate" token pricing could reset when lenders tighten.

### 5. NVIDIA Is Going Direct
Four of NVIDIA's biggest customers are building their own chips (e.g., OpenAI's inference chip). Barrie reads the $12.9B Hugging Face acquisition and the DGX Spark/Station line as Jensen hedging a data-center bust by selling hardware to end users, and betting on open models.

### 6. Jobs, AGI Hype and Energy
Barrie expects heavy white-collar dislocation (banks, law, call centers, commercial real estate), followed by an "everyone has a hustle" entrepreneurial economy. Winners have agency and initiative. He calls OpenAI's "AGI" Astra model mostly marketing. Energy is the "final boss": everyone burning 4B tokens/day would need ~30 TW. Humanoid robots (Unitree, Optimus) arrive within ~2 years.

interviewBody:
**Bottom line:** Recorded hours after the Fed's hawkish 25 bp hike, with dots signaling another hike before year-end. Bassman argues rising yields are about **trust, not inflation**: 10-year breakevens are pinned at ~2.34%, while a 6% deficit in peacetime and price-insensitive hyperscaler borrowing push nominal rates higher. Mortgage negative convexity is re-emerging as a bond-volatility accelerant.

### 1. The Hike Was About Credibility
Bassman had advocated a one-and-done 50 bp hike. The size barely matters economically; what matters is Warsh showing "an adult in the room." Warsh is also weaning markets off forward guidance and dot plots, which is like coming off a drug and is raising volatility. Bassman sees 25 bp plus a December hike as "torturing" the market for 12 weeks. A symbiotic, non-public Warsh–Bessent coordination is good enough to rebuild trust.

### 2. Why Trust Is Damaged
Corporate profits have doubled as a share of GDP (6% to 12%). The S&P has decoupled from Michigan sentiment (the "alligator jaws"). Housing affordability is the worst in 30 years, and the median first-home buyer's age jumped from ~33 to 38. Non-bank and private-credit lending is disintermediating banks and weakening Fed transmission.

### 3. Price-Insensitive Hyperscaler Borrowing
Projected hyperscaler debt issuance is approaching 30–35% competition with Treasury supply. These borrowers will pay 6%, 8%, 10% or 12% because they are in an existential race, a Global Crossing redux where only one or two winners emerge. Even so, he thinks hyperscaler **bonds are money good** thanks to core cash machines. The risk sits with equity holders, and AI-lab failures (e.g., Anthropic) are an equity problem, not a bond problem.

### 4. Slide 12: It's Not Inflation
Nominal yields are up ~150 bp, yet 10-year TIPS breakevens have averaged ~2.35% for four years and closed at 2.34%. If inflation were the driver, breakevens would widen. Bassman concedes CPI is "cooked" but concludes the move reflects concern about the US as a going concern and holding dollars, not runaway inflation.

### 5. The Mortgage Convexity Beast
A mortgage bond is effectively a covered call (long 10-year, short a 3-year call struck ~105). Three years ago the market's average price was ~$79, far from strike, so convexity was low. After "recouponing the stack" there are over $1T of Fannie 5.5s, and ~37% of the index carries 5%+ coupons, all very negatively convex. Current-coupon spreads have widened from the mid-90s to ~110 bp, driven by higher volatility and, more importantly, **yield-curve flattening**. Further flattening means more negative convexity and spillover into broader fixed income.

### 6. Fiscal Fixes, ETFs and Stablecoins
His fiscal predictions: uncap Social Security (now $184K), slowly raise the retirement age, means-test SS and Medicare, end step-up basis, revive some form of Simpson-Bowles, and pass "70/30" issues to rebuild confidence. On ETFs he warns about daily-reset leverage (volatility drag), return-of-capital high-yield products (10%+ yields are often your own money back), and liquidity mismatch in derivative-heavy ETFs if volatility spikes. He supports USD stablecoins as Treasury demand and calls Bitcoin a zero long-term. He doubts AI will eliminate human alpha soon because models react rather than predict.

interviewBody:
**Bottom line:** Oil's latest drop is "hope, not reality." Both wars (Iran and Russia-Ukraine) are closer to escalation than peace, and increasingly look like one conflict. Energy is becoming a tool of statecraft (diesel export curbs, an Americas-centred energy bloc), so rates and FX traders now have to think like oil traders. On the desk, the 10-year broke above 5% to its highest since 2007 even as crude fell ~$10.

### 1. Iran: Escalation, Not a Peace Deal
The US economic blockade is working, which pushes Iran to escalate militarily elsewhere through deniable proxies: the East-West pipeline, Yanbu, Bab el-Mandeb and the Houthis. Brent briefly hit ~$110. Every's base case is US escalation **after** the midterms (win or lose), likely with Israel and a GCC coalition. He calls the administration's "peace right after the election" line mirrored BS. Trump's foreign adversaries have every incentive to keep oil high into the vote, and a pre-election "Hail Mary" escalation is being discussed by serious people.

### 2. Energy as a Strategic Asset
Viewed "from outer space," the Americas plus the Middle East hold the energy that matters. If Trump topples Iran, the US gains huge leverage over China. If not, keeping the Middle East destabilized still leaves the Americas bloc relatively strong, even at a midterm cost.

### 3. Ukraine's Refinery Strikes and the Diesel Crisis
Days after Trump publicly warned against it, Ukraine hit Russian refineries (reportedly ~40% of diesel capacity). Record diesel prices worldwide are already causing social and political stress. Rabobank's energy team sees a genuinely serious diesel crisis as possible. Every suspects more layers than the headlines show: only Trump seems angry at Zelensky, and there are whispers that refined products still flow from Europe to Russia.

### 4. Diesel Export Ban and "NAPTHA"
The global energy market is still one integrated system even as everything else fragments. Every expects an Americas-centred closed loop (his joke: NAPTHA, the "North American Petroleum & Hydrocarbons Trading Hub Association") among countries aligned on China tariffs and defense. Tools include the Defense Production Act, mandated storage and selective export cuts. These need not be binary: Brazil (if Lula wins) or the Netherlands/Europe could be squeezed as leverage, which might push Europe to rein in Ukraine.

### 5. Greenland, China and Stablecoins
The new US–Denmark Greenland deal is permanent, survives Greenland independence, allows base expansion without a Danish veto, and gives the US a veto on third-party mineral and oil investment. Every calls it strategically huge and underreported. China wants both wars to end but doesn't want Russia or Iran to lose. The US reportedly offered only a 3–6 month extension of the trade truce, which suggests it expects to hold a stronger card soon. The CLARITY Act has stalled, but the DFC's new "SWORD" unit will make strategic supply-chain loans **in stablecoins**, so stablecoin statecraft is advancing outside Congress.

### 6. Part 2 Bonus ("MacroVoices Unplugged")
Politico reports a likely 90-day US diesel export ban, which Every expects would raise crude prices anyway through blowback. Canada's PM Carney ordered war-gaming of a US invasion scenario. Erik and Every also cover murkier Russia-Ukraine origins and AI as the new US–China Cold War, including China's possible strategy of copying and open-sourcing US frontier models. They close on talk of US nuclear first-strike options against Iran.

interviewBody:
**Bottom line:** Rosie isn't buying the inflation scare. Energy is a one-off "tax shock" that won't stick without wage pass-through, and wages are decelerating. The yield spike is ~90% real rates, driven by Fed **regime change** under Warsh plus hyperscaler borrowing. He circles **Nov 3 (midterms → gridlock)** and **Nov 4 (Treasury refunding)** as potential catalysts for a big bond rally, and is buying 2-year notes. Meanwhile the 10-year hit 5.30%+ and the median S&P stock is down ~16%.

### 1. Inflation Without Wages Isn't Sustainable
Rosenberg notes the tariff-inflation scare never materialized: core goods CPI went from 1.5% to below 0.7%, a 4-year low. Energy shocks act like a tax hike. Unless they feed wages (labor is ~30% of retail cost, six times more powerful than energy), they cause negative real wages and demand destruction in the other 80–85% of the basket. Unlike the 1970s (unions, COLAs) or 2021 (stimulus plus labor scarcity), wages today are decelerating. NY Fed's Williams (Sept 29) also sees no pass-through. Inflation is a rate of change: elevated but flat energy prices still fall out of the data.

### 2. Why Real Rates Are Rising
Three of the four biggest hyperscalers are now free-cash-flow negative and borrowing at the long end in multiple currencies, colliding with government supply. But debt went from $39T to $40T with nothing new, and the 10-year was below 4% in February at $39T. The big change is the Fed. Since Warsh took over in June the 10-year is up ~90 bp. Rosenberg criticizes Warsh's headline focus and his "share of PCE items rising >3%" metric (a bag of peanuts weighted the same as a car), the lack of a framework, and his abandonment of the Dallas trimmed mean (2.3%). Markets swung from pricing cuts in February to pricing 3–4 more hikes.

### 3. Midterms = Gridlock = Lower Yields
Democrats look likely to take the House, with >50% odds for the Senate in prediction markets. The One Big Beautiful Bill's one-off stimulus fades. Historically, a switch from one-party control to gridlock means slower growth, lower inflation and lower yields **80% of the time** over the following two years (e.g., 1994 Gingrich and the "mother of all bond rallies"). He is critical of policy incoherence: an affordability push, a trade war with Canada and a proposed $5,000 voter "dividend" (~$1T).

### 4. Nov 4 Refunding: Yellen 2023 Redux?
Bessent's $6B buybacks are a drop in the bucket in a $1T/day market. The real lever is supply mix. In November 2023, Yellen's shift toward bills triggered a ~100 bp 10-year rally in two months. Rosenberg expects Bessent may do similar after a comparable yield run-up.

### 5. Hidden Disinflation: China AI and Housing
Free Chinese open-source AI is another global disinflation force. Housing is in recession: new-home prices are down 8.5% y/y with 8.5 months of supply, and multifamily rents are deflating with no population growth. Plugged in real time, core CPI would be well below 2%. Under the surface the median stock is down ~15%, and Fed-sensitive sectors are already in correction. Bonds are hated and under-owned, like stocks in early 2009.

### 6. Gold: Correction in a Secular Bull
Gold has been hit by higher real rates and a stronger dollar, but the secular driver is intact: central-bank reserve reallocation. Gold's share of reserves is ~30%, versus 70% in 1980 and 10% in 1999. Rosenberg trimmed and is now adding again. The ROSIE ETF launched on the TSX on Sept 10, with a NYSE listing targeted for January–February 2027.

interviewBody:
**Bottom line:** The dollar-milkshake author was proven right again as the DXY closed above 102. Johnson expects a short-term dollar pullback and gold bounce, but higher dollars long-term. His "Disparate Housewives" thesis is that great-power competition with China will force a closer Fed–Treasury marriage. That opens tools like **marking US gold from $42 to market (~$1T credit to the TGA)** and stablecoins as the Treasury's own distribution rail. The US is the "big stack at the table" and can absorb higher rates better than everyone else.

### 1. Why the Dollar Broke Out
Warsh hiked to establish credibility instead of cutting. There is also nowhere else to go: Europe has a war on its border and no fiscal union, Japan has its problems and China is closed. The world earns, borrows and stores in dollars. A less-appreciated driver: AI growth may let the US "kick the can," so bondholders demand more yield, and every one of those trades needs dollars first.

### 2. Dollar and Gold Outlook
Momentum, positioning and narrative are stretched, so a short-term dollar pullback with euro and gold bounces is likely. Gold just printed a golden cross (50-day above 100-day). Longer term he sees much higher dollars: "heaven help the world" if it keeps rising without a pullback. If the DXY reaches 110, gold could drop to ~$3,700 (from ~$4,100), but he bought gold for a client this week and would buy any further low. The milkshake's sovereign-debt-crisis timing was wrong, but the asset directions were right.

### 3. "Disparate Housewives": The Fed–Treasury Marriage
The Fed has autonomy, not true independence. Fed–Treasury conflicts are common (1951 Accord; Powell hiking in 2022 while Yellen drained the TGA and RRP). Bessent has waded into monetary territory (buybacks, swap lines), and after saying "I am the house," he said **"we will work together"** with Warsh. Great-power competition will demand a united front, whether by hook or by crook.

### 4. Gold Revaluation and Stablecoins as Insurance Policies
The Treasury's gold certificates are carried at $42/oz. Marking them to ~$4,100 would credit the Treasury's Fed account with ~$1T in an afternoon. It's an accounting trick that debases the dollar, and it requires Fed cooperation, which is why the marriage matters. Stablecoins erode the Fed's leverage because they don't need the banking system to distribute debt or make payments. A gold-backed stablecoin can't be ruled out, nor can seizing the ~6,000 tons of foreign gold at the NY Fed "for services previously rendered." He doesn't expect any of this soon (the dollar is strong, so it isn't needed), but "the Fed has a lot more bullets than you can imagine."

### 5. What's Driving US Rates
Less enthusiasm for Treasuries (not outright rejection), AI growth expectations, and passive-flow mechanics in reverse: falling bond prices force systematic selling, which can create sharp dislocations. Rates are rising faster elsewhere (Europe, LatAm, Asia), so the US is the big stack at the table and can take pain while forcing others out. The trade: own USD and UST bills over CAD and Canadian bonds.

### 6. Cold War Analog, Republic to Empire, and AI
The best analog is the late 1940s and 1950s (high war debt plus a Cold War with China), not the 1970s. The US resembles late Republican Rome (foreign wars, inequality, personality cults), and what followed was the **Empire** under a strongman, not collapse. China is a formidable adversary: its electricity advantage matters in the AI race, and Johnson praised the Carly Anderson energy episode. He expects AI to be net positive long-term, with a bumpy transition likely handled through UBI or an expanded welfare state.

interviewBody:
**Bottom line:** Aalo plans to mass-produce 10 MWe sodium-cooled reactors (100 per year from a Texas factory). It says it can reach **coal and gas cost parity within the first few years of production**, much sooner than Erik expected. Its moat is running on commercially available LEU (5–8%), not scarce HALEU. Fuel recycling plus fast reactors would stretch known uranium from ~117 years to ~12,000. On the desk, a CoreWeave credit scare (bonds yielding ~15%) sparked the first real rotation out of AI into defensives, with long yields falling ~25 bp intraday.

### 1. Build the Same Good Reactor a Thousand Times
The industry spent 70 years trying to perfect ever-bigger one-off reactors, and Vogtle ran 2x over on time and budget. Aalo instead designs "the most power you can put on the back of a truck" and builds it repeatedly. Data centers are its "books" (the Amazon analogy) before expanding to every energy-importing market. Customers are asking to **reserve ~20% of factory output**, and reservations reaching ~80% would trigger factory #2.

### 2. The Pod and the Demand Gap
A pod is 50 MW: five reactors on one steam header with three 25 MW turbines. It delivers full nameplate output with one reactor or one turbine offline, designed for data-center "five nines" reliability behind the meter. Bank of America sees ~125 GW of data-center demand by 2030 against ~25 GW the grid can supply, a ~100 GW gap. One factory (1 GW per year) is a starting point to prove scalability, supply chain and fuel, not the end goal.

### 3. Path to Cost Parity
First-of-a-kind power costs mid-teens ¢/kWh, which is acceptable because early customers pay for **speed to power** and reliability. Aalo expects below 10¢ by the 10th reactor and coal and gas parity at ~50 reactors per year, within the first factory's first couple of years. Arafat agrees with Musk that mass manufacturing is ~10x harder than the prototype. The real bottleneck is the **supply chain** (230+ vendors who must scale with Aalo), so Aalo hires Tesla and EV volume-production veterans.

### 4. Fuel: LEU Now, Fast Reactors Later
Most advanced designs need HALEU (~4.5x the raw uranium and ~6x the SWU of LEU), which isn't commercially available for years. Aalo deliberately runs on 5–8% LEU uranium dioxide, so the existing mining, conversion, enrichment and fabrication chain can scale. Fabricators can roughly double output in existing plants. Known mines have only tapped ~30% of reserves (~117 years at once-through use). Recycling the 95% of "spent" fuel and moving to fast-spectrum reactors (60–100x more energy per mined pound) extends that to ~12,000 years. Aalo will switch once HALEU is unlocked, and Arafat thinks peers starting with fast reactors on day one are making a mistake.

### 5. "Waste" Is Used Fuel
Global spent fuel (~250K tonnes) is solid, cask-stored, has harmed no one in the commercial industry, and would fit on one football field one story tall. "The Simpsons did more damage to nuclear than any activist." Policy is improving: Energy Secretary Chris Wright backs recycling, and the DOE's **Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus (NLIC)** program will pick two host states for a cradle-to-grave fuel-cycle ecosystem. Erik cites the UK's 141 tonnes of reactor-grade plutonium slated for ~£4B geologic disposal as a wasted fuel resource.

### 6. China
China has more light-water reactors planned or under construction than the entire US fleet, runs an HTGR and is planning thorium molten-salt ships. Arafat argues every Chinese advanced design copies earlier US prototypes (52 reactors were built at Idaho National Lab), and that its pebble-bed plant struggles with first-of-a-kind issues. The US wins only by clearing policy bottlenecks and funding innovation. Aalo is closing its Series C (aalo.com).

interviewTitle: Dr. Anas Alhajji and Louis-Vincent Gave
interviewBody:
**Bottom line:** A double-header. Alhajji (just back from a Riyadh conference week held while the city was under attack) says the "three seas" crisis (the Gulf, the Red Sea and the Black Sea) has permanently changed energy. Crude is flowing again, but **products aren't**: only 25–35% of pre-war product volumes are moving through Hormuz. The diesel crisis will outlast the wars, and China holds the spare refining capacity. Gave says France is in an **emerging-market-style debt crisis** in a currency it can't print, with five crises at once and Le Pen polling in the mid-40s. His preferred hedges are positive-carry short-EUR trades.

### 1. Riyadh Energy Week: Security First
Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz: "There can be no energy future for all without energy security for all." The East-West pipeline has been expanded from 5.5 to 7 mb/d. The goal is ~10 mb/d of Hormuz bypass capacity, including a new pipeline through the Empty Quarter to Oman that Iraq and Kuwait could tie into (2–3 years), plus ~1.2 mb/d of temporary capacity by converting a gas line until May. The UAE is already building a second bypass. Alhajji called the conferences a logistics "masterclass," run with Riyadh's airport closed by attacks.

### 2. Crude Flows, Products Don't
US Energy Secretary Wright said Hormuz flows are back to 80–90% of pre-war levels (~13–14 mb/d), but **products are only at 25–35%**. That is the root of the diesel crisis: lost Gulf refining (e.g., UAE's Ruwais), export bans, rerouting, hoarding, and ~800K b/d of Black Sea diesel lost, which the media ignored for months. Germany now plans to **reopen closed refineries**. Aramco's Nasser: "There is no energy transition, only energy addition." Net zero means zero energy security. Countries are turning inward toward redundancy and import optionality, which means higher costs and more volatility than any outlook models. Turkey says desalination is now a power-demand driver.

### 3. Biofuels Compound It, and Demand Is Already Falling
The El Niño sugar crisis (India's worst cane crop in ~11 years) diverts cane from ethanol to sugar in India and Brazil. Low river levels in Europe and Indonesia are stranding barges, including palm oil for biodiesel. On demand, the IEA expected +160K b/d of US oil demand growth in 2026 and actual Jan–Jul growth is ~0. Global demand is declining in response to product prices. Recession has been masked by AI capex and EU fuel subsidies (~$16B extra in Q2), neither of which can last. Erik's scenario: crude stays near $100 while **crack spreads go to the moon**, and Alhajji agrees.

### 4. China and the Arctic
China keeps domestic product prices below world levels and controls export quotas (zero in October). Western refinery closures "enabled" its leverage. China benefits from Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb staying semi-closed because that promotes its Belt and Road alternatives. China–Russia Arctic shipping cooperation (Northern Sea Route oil and LNG near record highs) explains US interest in Greenland. Putin's proposed Trump–Xi–Putin summit without Zelensky goes nowhere without Europe: EU members board Russian tankers whenever Trump pressures Zelensky.

### 5. Gave on France
France has a three-bloc parliament that can't pass a budget, a ~5% deficit, taxes already at ~44% of GDP (past the Laffer peak), majority-foreign ownership of its debt, and debt in a currency it can't print. Clients now ask "who's stupid enough to own French bonds?" because holding them has become a career risk. A president with approval in the low teens has no authority while rioters, many from across Europe, run wild. Christophe Guilluy's three zones explain the politics: Zone A (city elites, EU flag, tennis), Zone B (suburban migrants, Palestinian flag, soccer) and Zone C (rural France, French flag, rugby). Zone A can no longer fund Zone B, so it turns to Zone C's protection. The only economic exits are retirement at 70 or a ~50% devaluation, and no candidate offers either. Mélenchon proposes default. Exiting the euro would blow up European insurers (France has more debt than all of Africa) and the derivatives books of SocGen, BNP and Crédit Agricole. Germany can't backstop this time (AfD, lunch eaten by China). Markets still price three ECB hikes, which Gave says will never happen.

### 6. Gave's Trades and the Tail-Risk Pile-Up
Short French/long German bonds costs ~150 bp of carry. Gave prefers **short EUR against NOK, ISK, HUF or GBP** (+150–500 bp carry, and NOK hedges an oil spike), long EUR/JPY or EUR/CNH vol (CNH vol near record lows), or long Asian FX versus EUR. Never in his career has he seen so many simultaneous coin-flip tail risks: France, energy, the end of AI capex, and a US market that's 50% tech plus communication services. Western governments are reaching the limit of cushioning consumers from the energy shock, and if the crisis runs into 2027 the question is who gets cut off: Sri Lanka, or the EU?

interviewBody:
**Bottom line:** Gromen's call that Hormuz could stay shut into July was mocked, and it has now lasted twice that long. The economic damage came slower than feared (Chinese demand cuts, SPR releases), but Iran only has to "beat the bond market," and US air-defense missile attrition favors Iran. His new worry is **AI-driven white-collar layoffs**: every 5% default rate on $19T of consumer debt equals ~40% of US bank equity. He holds ~30% cash/T-bills, would fade any bond rally, and expects the Fed to end up as the only Treasury buyer.

### 1. Why the Hormuz Shock Hasn't Hit Harder (Yet)
It's "Schrödinger's closure": Iran and the US both blockade, while Trump says it's open. Gromen underestimated how much China would cut demand and draw down its SPR, alongside coordinated Western SPR releases. Food impact is delayed: poorer farmers simply aren't buying unaffordable fertilizer, so the damage shows up as **lower 2027 crop yields**. That's bearish now and very bullish later. Diesel is near $200/bbl in places, and the market puzzle may be resolved by China quietly buying a lot of crude.

### 2. Iran's Strategy: Missile Math
Iran doesn't need to beat the US, just the bond market (the 10-year went from 3.94% in February to 5.3%). Illustratively, if the US can replenish ~100 air-defense interceptors a month while Iran forces it to fire 150–300, the US eventually runs dry, must pull assets from other theaters and looks weak. US bases have reportedly taken serious damage, and America hasn't fought without air superiority in 80 years, which makes a ground invasion untenable. Russia and China are happy to keep resupplying and targeting for Iran. Expect the war to drag on, hurting the administration into the vote.

### 3. The Strange 20 bp Bond Rally
Last Thursday the 10-year fell ~20 bp intraday, a move Gromen has seen only on catastrophe days (9/11, Lehman, COVID), and it broke the regime: gold down $50, oil up 3%, Bitcoin down 3–4%, the dollar up, yet yields down. Trump has repeatedly warned of a "1929-style depression" if Democrats win, and Bessent threatened to cram planned fiscal consolidation into November 4–January 3. Gromen speculates someone got a heads-up to "dump the board": stocks and commodities tank, so own bonds. He also notes reports that someone front-ran Trump's war tweets in oil, and that the CFTC was told to stand down. The FOMC (hold or +25 bp) matters little, and the 10-year has been pinned near 4.99% since.

### 4. The Second-Derivative AI Credit Problem
Layoffs are accelerating: Kroger (37% of corporate staff), AmEx (5%), Barclays (5%), and a Microsoft buyout of 27% of its workforce. That's the "we're gonna need a bigger boat" moment. Displaced white-collar workers won't find equal-wage jobs. US consumer debt is $19T, and **5% AI-driven defaults ≈ $1T ≈ 40% of US bank equity (~$2.6T)**. Banks would then cut lending, sell Treasuries or issue equity, all bad for risk. Consumer lenders and alt managers (COF, AXP, Blackstone, Blue Owl) are already badly lagging: "If AI works, why own this stuff?"

### 5. If the AI Credit Mania Breaks
AI is now "too big to fail," and contingency talk reportedly began in Washington a year ago. The administration also built a moat by banning DeepSeek from government work. A bust means recession and a deficit jump of 6–8% of GDP (+$1.8–2.4T). Add bank, foreign central bank (~$600B sold since February) and Cayman hedge-fund selling, and effective Treasury supply reaches ~$5T+. **The only buyer is the Fed**, through monetization in all but name, which needs a crisis first. So fade bond rallies unless the Fed or Treasury buybacks are involved.

### 6. The "Booby Prize": Social Unrest
Even if Bessent and Sacks keep the AI boom alive, a growing, heterogeneous US population losing good jobs is a recipe for unrest (see France, see Turchin's *End Times*). China, Japan and Korea have shrinking homogeneous populations. Gromen expects AI to be "litigated" in 2027 through political instability. Erik flagged Anthropic's S-1 warning that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks" as political ammunition.

interviewBody:
**Bottom line:** Democrats swept both chambers. Every says the bigger shock is geopolitical: a Congress hostile to foreign "adventures" makes the US a constrained, more isolationist hegemon, and power abhors a vacuum. Oil fell ~$18 peak to trough on peace hopes, which he calls "optimism, not realism." His base case is still escalation risk in the lame-duck window plus Russia stalling on Ukraine, which keeps crack spreads high. Bonds and the dollar barely moved, which Patrick reads as the market not buying a regime change.

### 1. A Constrained US Changes the World
"What happens in America doesn't stay in America." Wars are hard enough to win without fighting a political war at home. After January, the power of the purse and congressional opposition constrain US action. The spectrum runs from the "ultimate TACO / whole enchilada" (the US leaves the Middle East, so Iran, Russia, China and North Korea fill the vacuum) to Israel or Turkey stepping into the gap. **Neither argues for lower energy prices short term.** Israeli nuclear use is an extremely fat-tail risk: even in 1973 Golda Meir didn't reach for the button, and Israel may pivot toward India as an ally.

### 2. Data-Center Moratoria and Nuclear
Democrats (including "regime change in Texas") are pausing data centers over electric bills. Some build-out may have been fantasy anyway (water, copper, chips, power). If AI really is national security, pausing hands the lead to China. Erik notes that nuclear and uranium stocks fell harder than the market despite being the fix for the power problem. Every agrees: whoever has electricity has power, and that need won't go away.

### 3. Gridlock or Showdown?
The dollar is weaker (DXY ~101.18) on sheer uncertainty, since the range of policy outcomes has widened massively. Gold is up. Expect gridlock for now, but eventually generous Democratic spending bills. Trump isn't a lame duck: he keeps vetoes, executive orders and possibly Supreme Court support, while Congress is in its lame-duck phase now. A war-powers showdown could go to the Supreme Court, and either ruling is a big deal. Debt-ceiling brinkmanship follows a known playbook.

### 4. Escalation Risk Before January
Every's months-long base case was post-midterm escalation with Iran in the window before the new Congress, with French and British jets now in Saudi Arabia protecting Yanbu and Riyadh. Trump has "already received the kicking," so he could roll the dice. A token strike-and-retreat TACO is now more likely than before, but wouldn't lower energy prices sustainably. "Si vis pacem, para bellum": being anti-war doesn't prevent war for a hegemon. On Ukraine, Putin has every reason to stall because Trump will be weaker in six months. That means more Ukrainian refinery strikes and **crack spreads stay high**. At best a frozen, Korea-style conflict.

### 5. Tariffs: Window for a Bloc Bargain
Scrapping tariffs lowers costs short term but removes revenue and the main lever for re-industrialization, which supports the military-industrial base a hegemon needs. Every's hypothesis: Trump keeps China and transshipment tariffs and offers lower mutual tariffs to partners (e.g., Europe, close to its own China tariffs) who match a common external tariff. That would cut straight to a two-bloc world. Ag and fertilizer price transmission is delayed and complex, but could still show up with a lag if sulfur and energy disruption persist.

### 6. Cop Off the Beat
The US-built world order (WWII, Cold War) is crumbling, and an isolationist 1920s-style US means international "crime rates soar." Expect new flashpoints beyond the obvious ones. Trump may turn to executive actions, possibly bold affordability plays like homestead lotteries on federal land, and he won't seek a third term. A third party from disaffected MAGA figures (MTG, Tucker Carlson) has a clear chance of forming and a 0% chance of winning.

interviewBody:
**Bottom line:** Uranium prices keep climbing as fuel buyers turn bullish, but the mining shares have crashed back to Liberation Day lows because Wall Street baskets nuclear with the AI/data-center trade, and AI CapEx fears are high after the blue tsunami. Alkin says the thesis has nothing to do with AI: there isn't enough economically viable uranium for the existing ~440-reactor fleet plus ~80 reactors in the pipeline, utilities are contracting only about half their needs, and the cost curve has broken higher. Sentiment has split, with fuel buyers bullish and equities on fire sale. He calls the asymmetry "pretty remarkable" but warns you need a strong stomach.

### 1. AI Doesn't Matter, but the Market Thinks It Does
Alkin's thesis hasn't changed since uranium was $17–20/lb (now ~100+): supply can't meet demand from the existing fleet, and nuclear has gone from a ~0.5% grower to a 4–5% grower. "If a data center didn't open, there is still a massive structural deficit." But the banks' AI and momentum baskets lump nuclear in, so "facts be damned, it becomes flows." Some junior miners invited this by pitching themselves as AI plays.

### 2. Miners or Metal?
Mining is "exceptionally hard." Kazatomprom's IPO prospectus projected ~$14/lb costs by 2026; actual cost is **$38.45/lb**, or over $55 at the old tenge rate. Project after project misses: costs 80–200%+ above plan, production 50–70% below. That's bad for any one miner but bullish for price. Lower risk tolerance favors the physical metal; for torque, pay up for proven producers. Cameco's "miss" was noise. The key takeaway from its call was that it's getting **triple-digit pricing** while price reporters show $98–99, because they peg to the lowest offer heard, not where deals are struck. On Alkin's math Cameco trades at ~8–9× EBITDA vs. ~31× in 2022, when term uranium was ~$49.

### 3. No Bears Left at the Conference
Erik asked Alkin to recruit a uranium bear for a debate; he couldn't find one at the NEI fuel conference. For years fuel buyers ridiculed him and called for lower prices at every level. Now they concede prices are high but say new supply (NexGen, Denison, 2028–30) will fix it. Alkin says it won't. Fuel buyers are nuclear engineers who aren't paid to time the market, and fuel is only ~25% of a plant's cost (uranium alone mid-single to low-double digits), so they're not commercially driven.

### 4. Half-Contracting and a Broken Cost Curve
Utilities are contracting only a little over half their needs (deck slide 25) and drawing down inventories, yet the long-term price has quadrupled. Billions of pounds must be contracted by 2040 after 15 years of destocking, so restocking means buying well above consumption ("a pig through a python"). The forecasters' weighted-average cost curve went $24 (2019) → $27 → $30 → $38 (2025), the same as Kazatomprom's cost, the lowest in the world, so the curve "needs a reset" (slide 26). RFPs that used to draw 7–12 bidders now get few. The services already blew out: conversion went from $4 to $60+/kg and enrichment from 30 to 200+. "The product will catch up."

### 5. The Light-Water Leapfrog
Erik's scenario: factory-built Gen IV reactors (Aalo Atomics plans 100 a year from Georgetown, Texas; Valor Atomics and others) reach behind-the-meter users by ~2030, before any new AP1000. Alkin: then you "kiss your ass goodbye" on current price assumptions. Supply would have to come from tails, stockpiles and deeply uneconomic mines at much higher prices. Today: term ~$99, contract ceilings $150–160, floors $70–75, spot ~$91–92. The 2007 spot peak of $137 is ~$200 in today's dollars, and that came with a five-year surplus; today's outlook shows massive deficits. If panic hits, buyers will be late, as in conversion (~15×) and enrichment (~7×).

### 6. Surviving the AI-Bust Risk
Alkin avoids trade-structuring advice, but notes physical uranium isn't in the AI baskets. The upside catalyst is new-build announcements: there's talk of 10–20 reactors to be started by 2030, and a single utility signing on would likely bring several more. Erik pointed retail listeners to the ETFs and to SPUT at an ~18% discount to NAV. (Fund contact for accredited investors: ir@sachemcove.com.)
